Question Choices: What is the population in a statistical study?
Question Answers: the entire group of interest|all individuals of interest|the full group being studied
Hints: The population is broader than the sample.|It is the group the study aims to describe.
Solution: The population contains every individual the study aims to describe. A sample contains only selected members measured in the study; it is not the entire target population.

Question Answers: a subset of the population|part of the population
Hints: Researchers often cannot measure everyone.|They collect data from a smaller group.
Solution: A sample is the subset selected from the population for measurement. Researchers use its observations to learn about the wider group, while considering how the selection method may affect representativeness.

Question Choices: Select. Why is a random sample useful? ~~Less selection bias | Exact population proportions every time | Volunteers only~~
Hints: Selection should not favor one group.|Random choice improves representativeness.
Solution: Random selection gives population members a known chance of selection and reduces deliberate selection bias. A well-chosen sampling frame helps represent the intended population. Randomness does not guarantee a representative result or remove nonresponse and wording bias.

Question Choices: A school surveys only students leaving the gym about exercise habits. What bias may occur?
Hints: Gym users may exercise more than other students.|The sample underrepresents some groups.
Solution: Sampling only gym leavers excludes many other students and may overrepresent students who exercise frequently. This selection bias can prevent the sample from representing all students, even if many gym users respond.

Question Choices: Which study type assigns a treatment to subjects: observational study or experiment?
Hints: Researchers actively impose a condition.|Observational studies only observe.
Solution: An experiment deliberately assigns a treatment. A well-designed randomized controlled experiment compares treatments under similar conditions and uses random assignment to reduce confounding, supporting a causal conclusion about the treatment.

Question Choices: Which study type observes existing conditions without assigning treatment?
Hints: No variable is deliberately imposed.|Researchers record what already occurs.
Solution: In an observational study researchers measure existing conditions without assigning a treatment. Associations can be studied, but other explanations must be considered before claiming cause and effect.

Question Choices: A strong correlation between two variables proves causation. Enter True or False.
Hints: A lurking variable may affect both.|Association alone does not establish cause.
Solution: False. An association, even a strong one, does not itself establish causation. A third factor could influence both variables, or the causal direction could be different. Appropriate study design and evidence are needed.

Question Choices: What design feature helps separate a treatment effect from other influences?
Question Answers: random assignment|a control group|random assignment and a control group
Hints: Comparable groups support causal conclusions.|Random assignment balances other factors.
Solution: Random assignment helps balance other influences between treatment groups on average; a control group supplies a comparison under similar conditions. Together they help isolate treatment effects. Random assignment differs from random sampling and does not guarantee identical groups.

Question Choices: Select. To estimate average sleep for all students at a school, which sample is most reasonable? ~~A school-wide random sample | One convenient class | Volunteers reporting unusually little sleep~~
Hints: Include students from across the population.|Avoid sampling only one class or activity.
Solution: Use a sampling frame covering the whole school and randomly select students across grades. A single class or activity may systematically miss groups. Random sampling reduces selection bias but still allows chance variation and possible nonresponse bias.

Question Choices: Which can support a cause-and-effect conclusion more directly: a well-designed experiment or an observational study?
Hints: Look for random assignment and controlled treatment.|Observational studies can establish association.
Solution: An experiment deliberately assigns a treatment. A well-designed randomized controlled experiment compares treatments under similar conditions and uses random assignment to reduce confounding, supporting a causal conclusion about the treatment.
